analysis.one_liner: Blocks EPA from limiting power plant carbon emissions unless multiple agencies certify zero job, economic, or rate increases.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its initial committee referral and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to stop the EPA from issuing any rule or guidance limiting carbon dioxide emissions from any fossil fuel power plant, new or existing, until four separate certifications were in hand: the Department of Labor certifying no job losses anywhere, the Congressional Budget Office certifying no loss to GDP, the Energy Information Administration certifying no increase in electricity rates, and the grid regulators certifying no reliability effects [S2][S3]. Because some job shifting, economic change, or rate movement is nearly always measurable in an economy as large as the United States, these standards would have functioned as a near-permanent ban on federal carbon limits for power plants [S3]. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, where it stayed without any further action [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mining companies and coal-fired power plant operators would gain the most, since they would be permanently shielded from federal limits on carbon emissions and the compliance costs that come with them [S3]. Owners of fossil fuel plants generally would avoid retrofit or fuel-switching costs that carbon rules typically require.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal producers and fossil fuel plant owners

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any EPA rule or guidance limiting carbon dioxide emissions from a fossil fuel power plant — new or existing — until the Department of Labor certifies no employment loss, the CBO certifies no GDP loss, the Energy Information Administration certifies no electricity rate increase, and FERC and NERC certify grid reliability [S3].
Because it applies to plants that 'commence operation at any time,' it covers every existing coal and gas plant, not just future construction [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the health and climate costs of unchecked power plant carbon emissions, since the bill strips the EPA's existing Clean Air Act authority to limit them [S3]. Communities near polluting plants would continue to bear local air quality effects, and the costs of climate change fall broadly on the public rather than on any single payer.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through pollution and climate costs

drawbacks.text: The certification thresholds are effectively impossible to meet: proving that a nationwide carbon rule produces zero job losses, zero GDP change, and zero rate increase anywhere in the economy would allow a single contrary data point in any certification agency's analysis to block the rule indefinitely [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade-off: shielding coal jobs and electricity rates means leaving the carbon emissions that drive climate change unregulated at the federal level, and the bill addresses this cost by simply prohibiting the regulation rather than weighing it [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow to a specific industry — coal producers and fossil plant operators — in the form of avoided compliance costs, while the costs (continued carbon emissions and their associated health and climate effects) are spread across the public [S3]. The certification design is not a balanced weighing of costs; it is structured so that regulation cannot happen, since no large economy-wide rule could realistically be certified as producing zero job, GDP, or rate effects [S3]. The bill died without ever reaching a vote, so neither set of effects was realized through this legislation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Power Subcommittee on June 3 and 5, 2015, and sat there with no markup, no vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Mike Kelly of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on June 3, 2015, with Bob Latta and Brett Guthrie as the only cosponsors, both Republicans [S3][S4].

The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and to the Energy and Power Subcommittee two days later; the action record shows no further activity of any kind [S5].
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, without the bill ever receiving a committee vote or floor vote, so the Clean Air Act was never amended as the bill proposed [S3][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, the existing Clean Air Act authority for EPA to regulate power plant carbon emissions was left intact. Coal operators did not receive the shield the bill would have provided, and the public did not lose the legal basis for federal carbon rules through this legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public's existing EPA authority stayed intact

for.name: Mike Kelly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to block EPA carbon limits for power plants pending multi-agency certification.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in the 114th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 3, 2015, and never scheduled a markup, vote, or floor action on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were all Republicans, with no Democratic support in the record, and the bill never reached a vote where broader party positions would have shown [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Coal mining and coal-fired power generation
industries.note: The bill would have permanently barred federal carbon limits covering every existing and future fossil fuel plant, sparing coal operators the compliance costs of emission controls while the public continued to bear the pollution and climate effects [S3]. Its gain runs directly against the public interest the Clean Air Act regulates [S3].

Fossil plant owners would avoid carbon compliance costs and potential rate impacts, but utilities that had already begun shifting toward gas and renewables would face a rule freezing the regulatory landscape in favor of coal. The bill was referred to the subcommittee covering electricity issues and never acted on [S5].

industries.industry: Renewable energy and clean power industries
industries.note: Blocking carbon limits for power plants would remove a key policy driver pushing electricity generation toward lower-emission sources, weakening the market conditions under which renewables expand. The bill's failure left that policy landscape unchanged [S3].
